summary: Research by scientists like Toshiyuki Nakagaki has shown that the single-celled slime mould Physarum polycephalum can solve mazes and efficiently navigate networks, sparking a fierce debate in biology. While traditionalists argue that true cognition and intelligence require neurons and brains, a growing group of biogenic theorists contend that intelligence is an intrinsic trait of all life, including cells and plants. This shifting perspective challenges long-held human assumptions about intelligence and cognition.
key_points: Toshiyuki Nakagaki's experiments demonstrated that the slime mould Physarum polycephalum can solve mazes and map efficient transit routes.
Traditional scientists ("neuropurists") argue that intelligence strictly requires brains and neurons, dismissing claims of plant or cell cognition.
Biogenic theorists believe that cognition and intelligence are fundamental traits shared by all living organisms, including single cells and plants.
Slime moulds are neither fungi, plants, nor animals, and their complex behaviors—such as decision-making and memory—continue to challenge scientific definitions.

title: Cancer-fighting T cells need small amounts of ROS to attack tumors, study finds
author: Oregon Health; Science University Reviewed
content:
New research reveals a promising new target for treating cancer by harnessing a type of molecule previously thought to do more harm than good. 
For decades, reactive oxygen species, or ROS, often called free radicals, have been viewed primarily as harmful molecules linked to aging, DNA damage and cancer. A new study co-led by Oregon Health & Science University finds that cancer-fighting T cells need small amounts of ROS to attack tumors. 
The investigators discovered that cancers exploit the T cell need for ROS by releasing an antioxidant protein that removes ROS from the tumor environment, effectively shutting down the attack by the immune system upon the cancer. 
Published today in the journal Science, the findings identify a previously unknown way tumors escape immune attack and point to a promising new target for cancer immunotherapy. 
The research was co-led by physician-scientist Robert L. Eil, M.D., associate professor of surgery in the OHSU School of Medicine and member of the OHSU Knight Cancer Institute, alongside investigators at the University of Cambridge. 
One of the surprising findings is that antioxidants aren't always beneficial in the context of cancer. While reactive oxygen species sound threatening, T cells actually need them to perform their tumor-fighting job. What we found is that tumors can exploit the T cell's dependency by removing the reactive oxygen species the immune system depends on." 
Robert L. Eil, M.D., associate professor of surgery, OHSU School of Medicine
By analyzing tumor interstitial fluid, the liquid that surrounds cells within tumors, researchers found that tumors create an antioxidant-rich environment that essentially chemically "smothers" T cells. The team identified high levels of an antioxidant enzyme known as peroxiredoxin-1, or PRDX1, which neutralizes the ROS within the tumor microenvironment, depriving the T cells of the signals they need to activate and attack cancer cells. 
"We tend to think of reactive oxygen species purely as damaging byproducts of metabolism. But we are increasingly understanding that ROS have important functions within cells, and T cells require them to activate," said Alexander J. Wesolowski, Ph.D., first author of the study and a researcher in the Department of Pathology at the University of Cambridge. "Our study develops this picture, revealing that tumors can exploit this very dependency to evade elimination." 
How tumors silence T cells 
The findings may also help explain a long-standing mystery in cancer research. 
To determine whether PRDX1 directly contributes to tumor immune evasion, researchers used CRISPR gene-editing technology to create cancer cells that could no longer produce antioxidant protein. 
Removing PRDX1 enhanced immune activity and reduced tumor growth in multiple experimental models. In one melanoma model, tumors lacking PRDX1 were spontaneously rejected by the immune system. In others, eliminating PRDX1 made previously resistant tumors responsive to immune checkpoint blockade, a form of immunotherapy that helps T cells recognize and attack cancer. 
The research team also investigated whether the same mechanism occurs in people. They analyzed published datasets from human cancer cell lines, examined gene activity across thousands of human tumors and measured PRDX1 in fluid collected from patient tumors. Across all three approaches, researchers found evidence that human cancers also release PRDX1 into their surroundings, where it can suppress T cell activity. 
The findings are especially significant because many cancers either do not respond to immunotherapy or eventually develop resistance. 
"The immune system has already shown us that it can eradicate advanced cancers in some patients," Eil said. "The challenge is that current immunotherapies don't work for most people, and even when they do, complete responses remain relatively uncommon. The more we understand how tumors suppress T cells, the more opportunities we have to design therapies that reverse that suppression." 
Researchers describe PRDX1 as part of a previously unrecognized "redox checkpoint," a mechanism by which tumors manipulate ROS levels to suppress anti-tumor immunity. The study found that cancer cells increase PRDX1 expression during a process known as immunoediting, in which tumors evolve under pressure from the immune system and acquire characteristics that help them escape immune attack. 
Considering future therapies 
Researchers are considering how they might be translated into future therapies. 
Potential approaches include drugs that neutralize tumor-derived antioxidants, therapies that block PRDX1 activity and engineered immune cells designed to resist the suppressive effects of antioxidant-rich tumor environments. 
"What's exciting is that we've identified a target nobody was really looking for before," Eil said. "This doesn't put a drug in patients' hands tomorrow, but it gives us an entirely new pathway to pursue. Discovering new targets is how future treatments begin." 
Eil said his team and collaborators will continue studying how tumors suppress immune responses and how those mechanisms can be overcome through next-generation immunotherapies, including engineered T cell therapies.
"This is one more victory against ignorance in understanding why cancers are so difficult to treat," Eil said. "Every time we uncover a new way tumors suppress the immune system, we gain another opportunity to fight back. That's how better treatments are built." 
 In addition to OHSU and the University of Cambridge, the study included researchers from the Babraham Institute in England, the University of Tübingen, Germany, the University of Lausanne, Switzerland, the Humanitas Clinical and Research Center, Italy, and other collaborating institutions. 
Source:
Journal reference:
Wesolowski, A. J., et al. (2026). Tumor-derived antioxidants suppress immunity by depriving T cells of reactive oxygen species. Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adz8203. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adz8203
summary: New research reveals that cancer-fighting T cells require small amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS), or free radicals, to effectively attack tumors. However, tumors exploit this dependency by releasing an antioxidant protein called PRDX1 that neutralizes ROS and suppresses the immune response. Removing PRDX1 in experimental models enhanced immune activity, reduced tumor growth, and made resistant tumors responsive to immunotherapy, identifying a promising new target for cancer treatment.
key_points: T cells need small amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS) to activate and attack tumors.
Tumors evade the immune system by releasing an antioxidant enzyme called PRDX1, which neutralizes ROS in the tumor environment.
Using CRISPR to remove PRDX1 in experimental models enhanced immune activity and reduced tumor growth.
Analysis of human cancer data indicates that human cancers also release PRDX1 to suppress T cell activity.
The discovery points to potential new therapies, such as drugs that neutralize tumor-derived antioxidants or block PRDX1 activity.

title: After 8 years, Europe's BepiColombo mission is on final approach to Mercury
author: Stephen Clark
content:
The BepiColombo mission cleared a major milestone this week in the final stretch of an eight-year interplanetary voyage to Mercury, the hard-to-reach, scorching hot iron world at the Solar System’s innermost frontier.
The robotic science mission, with a price tag of nearly $2 billion, is led by the European Space Agency with contributions from Japan and the United States. Since its launch in 2018, BepiColombo has spiraled closer to the Sun using a combination of plasma propulsion and a series of flybys of Earth, Venus, and Mercury. The maneuvers changed the spacecraft’s velocity and steered it toward a final encounter with Mercury later this year.
Next time it reaches Mercury, BepiColombo will be traveling at just the right speed for the planet’s gravity to capture the spacecraft into orbit. Scientists working on interplanetary missions are accustomed to long waits for scientific payoffs. It took nearly 10 years for NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft to travel from Earth to Pluto. It turns out traveling to fleet-footed Mercury and then entering orbit requires more energy, or delta-v, than sending a probe to fly by Pluto.
That’s why BepiColombo’s trajectory required an unprecedented nine planetary flybys, or gravity assists, to set up for the chance to enter orbit around Mercury later this year. BepiColombo also launched with the most powerful electric propulsion system ever put into deep space, with four gridded ion thrusters to reshape its orbit around the Sun in between flybys.
BepiColombo is now a few months from reaching the end of its journey, and it no longer needs the plasma engines. On Thursday, BepiColombo jettisoned the section of the spacecraft containing the ion the thrusters. This part of the spacecraft, called the Mercury Transfer Module, was responsible for generating power and providing propulsion for BepiColombo throughout the eight-year cruise.
summary: The BepiColombo mission has reached a major milestone in its eight-year journey to Mercury by jettisoning its ion propulsion module. Led by the European Space Agency with Japanese and U.S. contributions, the nearly $2 billion robotic spacecraft used nine planetary flybys and an electric propulsion system to navigate toward Mercury. Later this year, the spacecraft will use Mercury's gravity to enter orbit.
key_points: The BepiColombo mission is an eight-year interplanetary voyage to Mercury led by the European Space Agency with contributions from Japan and the US.
The spacecraft successfully jettisoned its Mercury Transfer Module, which provided power and ion propulsion during the journey.
Reaching and entering orbit around Mercury required an unprecedented nine planetary flybys and the most powerful electric propulsion system ever used in deep space.
The spacecraft is scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury later this year.

title: Why Hasn't Amazon Launched Its Leo Satellite Internet Service Yet?
author: Michael Kan
content:
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/t/pcmag_uk/news/w/why-hasnt-/why-hasnt-amazon-launched-its-leo-satellite-internet-service_b1ds.1920.jpg) (Credit: PCMag/Michael Kan)
Amazon's Starlink competitor, Leo, was supposed to launch in mid-2026, but it’s now September, and so far, the satellite internet service has been quiet. What’s up?
The company tells PCMag it’s still waiting for all the satellites to reach their assigned operating orbits, so Leo will have enough network capacity and coverage when it officially launches.
In July, Amazon hit a crucial milestone when it sent another 29 Leo satellites into space, bringing the total deployed in Earth’s orbit to 396. That's enough to kick off "initial service," Chris Weber, VP for Amazon Leo, said at the time. But even after entering space, some of the satellites still need to reach an altitude of around 600 kilometers, where they’ll orbit and beam high-speed internet data to users on the ground.
Tracking from astronomer Jonathan McDowell shows that only 299 of the Leo satellites have reached operational orbit. Another 78 appear to be descending or ascending into position. Meanwhile, a separate group of 14 satellites seems to be relocating and remains close to the operational orbits. (The rest have been or are in the process of being retired.) 
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/pcmag_uk/photo/l/leo-graph/leo-graph_vcwm.jpg)
McDowell estimates most of the functioning satellites will reach the operational orbits by November, but some will take longer. “Their protocols may just involve a lot of preliminary testing," he told PCMag in an email. "And Starlinks often take several months to orbit raise, too.”
Amazon didn't comment on when Leo will begin service or when more satellites will exactly launch. The last one took place two months ago. But the company noted that United Launch Alliance is preparing to launch a batch of satellites using its heavy-lift Vulcan Centaur rocket. Amazon has also shipped another batch to French Guiana for a seperate mission using Arianespace.
For now, the Leo constellation is relatively small compared with Starlink, which operates about 10,000 satellites in orbit. Satellite industry analyst Carlos Placido also expects Leo to offer service only in certain areas or latitudes once it launches, citing the limited density of its satellite constellation. ![](https://sm.pcmag.com/pcmag_uk/photo/l/leo-sat/leo-sat_w6ky.jpg)
The first-gen Leo constellation is supposed to span 3,232 satellites, and even then, it won’t cover the polar regions. A second-gen network is in the works to add even more capacity and coverage.
As it waits for its satellites to reach the right orbits, Amazon says it continues to expand network testing with employees and select enterprise customers in a closed beta. The company plans on sharing more news soon. Pricing hasn't been announced, but Amazon has suggested it’ll be competitive with Starlink, which already has over 13 million customers worldwide.
summary: Amazon has delayed the official launch of its Leo satellite internet service while it waits for deployed satellites to reach their assigned operating orbits. Although Amazon has sent 396 satellites into space, astronomer tracking indicates that only 299 have reached operational altitude as of September. Meanwhile, the company is conducting closed-beta network testing with employees and select enterprise customers.
key_points: Amazon's Leo satellite internet service launch has been delayed as the company waits for satellites to reach operating orbits.
Amazon has deployed 396 satellites into space, but only 299 have reached their operational orbit around 600 kilometers.
Astronomy tracking and expert estimates suggest most functioning satellites will reach operational orbits by November or later.
Amazon is currently conducting closed-beta network testing with employees and select enterprise customers.
The first-generation Leo constellation is planned to include 3,232 satellites, which is significantly smaller than Starlink's constellation.

title: How to future proof your wrists
author: David Cox
content:
How to future proof your wrists
![Getty Images Two men arm wrestling (Credit: Getty Images)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p80mnn.jpg.webp) Getty Images
Modern life is ruining our wrists. We can all do something about it, but it helps to start early.
It began with a dull ache. Over the course of a summer, it rapidly progressed to an arm-juddering pain, radiating through my left hand every time I struck a tennis ball or even attempted to open a door.
I was 18 at that point, and playing competitive tennis was an important part of my life, but I'd just experienced an injury that would plague me for years. Now, nearly two decades later, it could increase my risk of developing wrist arthritis. Such problems are surprisingly common in mid to later life.
Our wrists are remarkably adaptable. They have the strength to allow us to lift heavy objects (including the World Record of 2,422 kg (5339 lbs)), the flexibility to enable us to hit rogue balls during racquet sports, and the fine control to make tasks like painting possible.
From typing to holding a coffee cup, functional wrists are essential to normal everyday life. But they are easily damaged, and we all need to start thinking about them earlier in life than you’d expect. Here's how to protect yours, so you can continue taking them for granted for years to come.
A fragile balance
We may think of the wrist as a single joint, but it is actually a complex, comprising multiple smaller joints. These are formed of eight small bones known as the carpal bones, the two long bones of the forearm, and the bases of the five metacarpal bones within the palm.
"Every ligament and every bone in the wrist that connects it to your forearm bones are really in a very finely-tuned balance," says Andrew Abadeer, an assistant professor at the University of South Florida. "When that goes awry, that's when wrist arthritis starts to develop."
Simply avoiding arthritis is a major reason for maintaining your wrist health. There are many different kinds, but it typically takes one of three forms: rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or post-traumatic arthritis. The latter two ailments occur when the cartilage cushioning the small bones within the wrist becomes damaged, or the bones become misaligned. Both are linked to the long-term effects of injuries to the ligaments and bones within the wrist, or lingering inflammation due to overuse through repetitive manual tasks.
Sara Larsson, a researcher who studies wrist rehabilitation at Lund University, explains that this trauma may be as simple as a repetitive twisting movement or tripping and falling on an outstretched hand. "I see many people who had an injury when they were young, everything appeared to be fine again, and then 20 years later, they develop problems."
Arthritis of the wrist has been estimated to affect as many as one in seven Americans. It is not only highly painful, but makes it harder for people to dress themselves and cut their own food, with the psychological burden being linked to depression.
Abadeer describes the wrist as being a "sentinel joint" which can reflect early signs of declining health within the rest of the body. About half of all patients who develop rheumatoid arthritis first feel the effects the disease in their wrist before it progresses to other joints. Because the brain devotes a large region of the cortex, known as the cortical homunculus, to mapping the hands, wrist and fingers, grip strength can reflect brain structure and cognitive health.
But people who reach their sixties with their wrists in better shape – typically assessed in the form of grip strength – tend to have better health overall. Those people are not only less frail and less vulnerable to falls, bone fractures and osteoporosis – a condition that weakens bones. But they are less likely to lose their independence in older age.
Setting yourself up
Before we get started, Jaehon Kim, an orthopaedic surgeon at the Ichan School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, recommends considering your diet. Foods high in calcium and other minerals, such as small, bony fish (sardines work well for this) and dairy products can help to mitigate against the development of osteoporosis. In addition, while weight might not seem particularly related to wrist health, shedding excess body fat can improve the overall biomechanics of the wrist joint.
But overall, Larsson says that the best preventative measure is to do a few simple home-based workouts which can help make your wrist more resilient and stave off problems further down the line. For each of the below exercises, she recommends performing three sets of 10 repetitions (this means performing the exercise 10 times, resting, performing it again 10 times, resting, and doing it another 10 times), three or four times per week.
If you have any pre-existing conditions or injuries, it's important to seek medical advice before starting a new exercise regime. And if you feel pain at any point, stop and seek medical help.
1. Build your shoulder muscle strength
The main muscles in your shoulders are known as the deltoids. While they may appear unrelated to wrists, Larsson says that strengthening the muscle groups across the whole arm can greatly benefit your wrist as they work together like a chain.
"You don't just use your hand, you use the whole arm," says Larsson. "And if you're weak in your shoulders, then you put more load on the wrist. But if you are strong, then you can protect and unload the wrist."
One easy method of training your shoulder muscles is simply to stand with your arms out to the sides, with your arms either straight or slightly bent. Slowly raise your arms up to the ceiling and then bring them down again slowly. Repeat this ten times.
2. Strengthen your grip
Grip strengthening exercises can improve wrist stability by conditioning groups of forearm muscles known as flexors and extensors, which attach to your fingers across the wrist joint, allowing you to grip objects. Studies have previously shown that this can also help people with existing wrist pain.
"All your forearm muscles connect into your hand on both sides of your wrist in a pulley system," says Abadeer.
To work these muscles, you ideally want a hand therapy ball or therapeutic putty – a silicone-based material which you can squeeze in your hand – but a tennis ball will do.
![Getty Images Even healed wrist injuries can lead to problems decades later (Credit: Getty Images)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p7zc9q.jpg.webp) Getty Images
Hold the ball or putty in the palm of your hand and squeeze it as hard as you can for five to 10 seconds. Release the grip and relax your hand for another five seconds and then squeeze again. Repeat ten times in each hand. (Read more from the BBC about how grip strength can predict your chances of living to 100.)
3. Gently load and flex the wrist
According to Kim, another key means of reducing the stress on the wrist joints and tendons is exercises that flex and extend the wrist, using some form of mild weight or resistance as a load.
This can also strengthen bones in the wrist, which could have longer-term health benefits, particularly when it comes to preventing a type of osteoporosis known as disuse osteopenia. "When they're loaded, these bones strengthen and start to remodel, adding more strength to the wall of that bone," says Abadeer.
To do this, start by sitting and resting your forearm on a table with your hand hanging off the edge and holding a small weight, between 3 and 7kg (5 and 15lb). For a flexion exercise, have your palm facing upwards and curl your wrist up toward your body before lowering it back down again. For an extension exercise, have your palm facing downwards while holding the weight, and lift your hand up towards the ceiling before lowering it down again.
If you don't have weights, Larsson suggests using a resistance band instead. Fix one end of the band under a table leg and hold the other end across your wrist so you're experiencing some resistance while carrying out the exercises.
Repeat both flexion and extension ten times. "I think this can go a long way in terms of helping the joints in your wrist, especially if you're typing and writing a lot," says Kim.
4. Supinate and pronate
Lastly, there are supination and pronation movements. These can improve the range of motion of your wrist and its overall functionality. Like the flexion and extension exercises, they can be carried out over a table with a small weight or resistance band.
Begin with your hand over the edge of the table with your thumb pointing up. Then slowly turn your wrist so your palm faces down, then return to the starting position, and rotate the other way so your palm faces up. Repeat this ten times.
More like this:
Abadeer says that such exercises are becoming increasingly important as we now live in what he describes as "a pronated world", where our hands spend many hours of the day in a fixed position, either due to typing on a laptop or a phone.
As with all our joints, strong, flexible wrists are something that we often take for granted. But as I found myself when my wrist was out of action for many months, it's only when you lose something that you realise its true importance.
* All content within this article is provided for general information only, and should not be treated as a substitute for the medical advice of health care professionals.
**A previous version of this article included an incorrect figure for the heaviest weight ever lifted.
--
For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.
summary: The wrist is a complex, finely-tuned joint structure that is vulnerable to long-term damage from repetitive tasks, overuse, or past injuries, potentially leading to conditions like arthritis later in life. Maintaining wrist health through diet, reducing excess body fat, and performing targeted exercises can improve resilience, protect against injuries, and preserve overall independence. Simple home-based workouts focusing on the shoulders, grip strength, wrist flexion and extension, and supination and pronation can help future-proof your wrists.
key_points: Wrist arthritis and trauma can stem from simple, early-life injuries or repetitive movements that surface decades later.
Good grip strength in later life is linked to better overall health, cognitive health, reduced frailty, and lower risk of falls and bone fractures.
Dietary considerations, such as consuming foods high in calcium and minerals and shedding excess body fat, help improve overall wrist biomechanics and mitigate osteoporosis.
Targeted home exercises focusing on shoulder strength, grip conditioning, mild wrist loading, and range-of-motion movements can protect and strengthen the wrist joint.

title: Cave art discovery suggests first humans in Ireland came from Wales
author: Neil Prior
content:
![At a secret location on a hillside in south-west Ireland,  a roughly circular natural cave entrance with moss-covered limestone surrounds, covered with ferns, ivy  and brambles.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/0e01/live/e9948ee0-a885-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.png)
Researchers have helped to unearth the earliest known evidence of human existence in Ireland
- Published
Researchers believe the first known humans to set foot on Ireland thousands of years ago were most likely from Wales, following the "exciting" discovery of ancient cave art.
During the most recent Ice Age, when much of the British Isles were beneath a vast continental glacier, the depleted sea levels opened a "lost land bridge" between modern-day Pembrokeshire and the south-east tip of Ireland, around Rosslare.
According to rock expert Dr George Nash, from Liverpool University, the opportunities presented by this pathway would have been too good for hunter gatherers to ignore.
Now, alongside an international team of experts, Nash has located eight cave sites in south-west Ireland featuring rock art dating back from at least 15,000 years ago, around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.
Nash, who coordinated the Lost Land Bridge Project, said there would have been a forested and grassland plateau around 46 miles (76 km) coast-to-coast.
With summertime temperatures typically -10Â°C to -20Â°C, Nash said the pathway would have supported wild horses, mammoth, bison, reindeer and other large herbivores, which fed off the hardy sedges, mosses and lichens growing through the fertile, but near-frozen soil.
Nash said he had always believed - from what he had gleaned throughout his career about human movement during the period - that it was inconceivable that people would not have utilised the opportunity the pathway presented.
This led him to assemble his multi-disciplinary team of experts from University College Dublin and the University of Adelaide, along with academics from Dubai, Wales and Portugal.
![Roughly a meter long, an engraving on the interior limestone wall of a cave in south-west Ireland shows a crude representation of a deer's head, neck and flank. An archaeologist holds up a ruler beneath the artwork in order to give a perspective of scale to its dimensions](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/da0c/live/285948a0-a886-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.png)
An engraving depicting the front quarters of a cervid deer, in a cave in south-west Ireland
"Up until now the earliest evidence archaeologists had found - through accidental discovery - was from around 10,500 years ago, but everyone - not just me - knew that simply couldn't have been correct.
"We just weren't looking hard enough, and not in the right places. The principle we worked on was 'absence of proof isn't proof of absence'."
He said advances in artificial intelligence (AI) had been a game-changer.
"With the help of caving specialist Shane Diffily and digital mapping consultant Darren Lee, we were able to fill a computer algorithm with everything we knew about the characteristics of cave dwellings in south Wales and set it to work searching for similar sites in Ireland, without us trudging blindly around the countryside, hoping to bump into something which looked promising."
![Shown in black and white: a series of parallel diagonal lines etched into a limestone wall, which in subsequent millennia have been covered in a calcified coating](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/489/cpsprodpb/5fad/live/52a70e80-a886-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.jpg)
This most primitive series of lines drawn on the wall of Bacon Hole Cave comes from the Gower Peninsula, which humans first occupied around 40,000 years ago
What their computer model spat out was 28 potential caves in south-west Ireland which the team investigated.
Eight of them were found to have cave art which they believe dates from at least 15,000 years ago and possibly much earlier, and around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.
The team are currently unwilling to be more precise about the location of the caves, for fear that they may be vandalised or looted.
![Lit from behind the photographer's beam illuminates the image of what Dr Nash believes to be a mammoth. With its head to the right, a curved tusk is prominent](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/cc4b/live/5e415520-a886-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.png)
This image of a mammoth on the limestone wall of a south-west Ireland cave dates from at least 20,000 years after early humans arrived in Wales
"We know that modern day south Wales was settled from around 35,000 to 40,000 years ago, by intrepid early modern humans from southern England, France and Spain, crossing the then dried-up land bridges of the English and Bristol Channels - seasonally settling in caves along the inhabitable strip of land stretching from Chepstow to St Davids," said Nash.
"Over 20,000 years their art progressed from primitive line drawings which may have been early tally charts, to more figurative and representative depictions of the world around them, and what we've found in Ireland is yet another progression from that."
The rock art which the Lost Land Bridge Project has uncovered includes engravings on the cave walls, paintings in ochre and charcoal and line sketches indented into clay and earth by fingertips.
![Concentric semicircles in now-hardened clay, flutings appear like the dirty smudges on a smartphone screen after swiping. They have a child-like appearance of rays emitting from a sun](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/b90f/live/8aab9260-a886-11f1-96fc-dd627484b0e6.png)
Probably not intended to be permanent at the time, made by three or four fingers gouged into soft layers of cave walls, flutings were probably early human children's initiation into interpretive rock art
Nash believes the growing population put pressure on humans to move ever more west and northwards.
"There were around 100 human-inhabited caves on The Gower Peninsula for example, in a time when the technology didn't yet exist for human groups to create their own free-standing dwellings.
"The ambient temperature within these caves would have remained between 10Â°C and 15Â°C all year round, so with bearskin covers and fires at the entrance - which also helped to ward-off predators - it would have been quite a cosy place to live, especially compared with the -20Â°C outside.
"Competition for these caves would have been intense.
"As family networks grew, knowledge of how to survive by following animal migration routes improved and they must have become bolder."
![An archaeologist wearing a helmet, red boiler suit and black gloves, measures a ceiling artwork within a cave in south-west Ireland](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/cb74/live/a91d74c0-a886-11f1-96fc-dd627484b0e6.png)
Nash says competition to live in these caves would have been intense
The Lost Land Bridge Project team believe the potential for more future discoveries is high.
"The sites we've currently explored are in south-west Ireland, but it's illogical to presume that early humans just bypassed Wexford, Waterford and Cork, and ploughed on west," said Nash.
"There must be more, and even earlier places which are just waiting for us to find them. This project is now pushing the boundaries of what we consider to be the final vestiges of a north-west European frontier. It's all very exciting."
summary: Researchers have discovered ancient cave art in south-west Ireland dating back at least 15,000 years, pushing back the timeline of human presence in the region by approximately 5,000 years. Led by Dr George Nash, the Lost Land Bridge Project used artificial intelligence to locate the cave sites, which they believe were reached by hunter-gatherers crossing a land bridge from Wales during the Ice Age. The newly found rock art includes engravings, ochre and charcoal paintings, and finger-indented sketches depicting animals and symbols.
key_points: Researchers discovered eight cave sites in south-west Ireland containing rock art dating back at least 15,000 years.
The findings suggest the earliest humans in Ireland likely originated from Wales, crossing a lost land bridge created by lowered sea levels during the Ice Age.
An artificial intelligence computer model helped the international team identify potential cave locations by analyzing characteristics of cave dwellings in south Wales.
The uncovered art features engravings of animals such as deer and mammoths, as well as paintings in ochre and charcoal and finger sketches.

title: In 2002, Lundy began its rat-eradication project; puffins later rose from 13 in 2000 to 1,335, and more than 40,000 seabirds now nest on the island
author: TOI Science Desk
content:
Off the coast of southwest England, the small island of Lundy was once a textbook case of how invasive rats can devastate seabird colonies. By the late 1990s, puffin numbers had crashed to just 13 breeding pairs, and many other seabirds had abandoned the island altogether. In 2002, conservationists launched an ambitious rat-eradication project to give the islandâs wildlife a second chance. More than two decades later, the results are striking: puffins have rebounded to 1,335 individuals, and over 40,000 seabirds now return each year to nest on Lundyâs cliffs and burrows. As documented by the Lundy Field Society and The Landmark Trust, the islandâs transformation shows what is possible when a community commits to removing a single, destructive invasive species.
An island under siege
Lundy, about 12 miles off the Devon coast, has long been a haven for seabirds. Its steep cliffs, grassy slopes and isolated location make it ideal for species such as puffins, guillemots, razorbills, Manx shearwaters and storm petrels. Historically, tens of thousands of birds nested there, filling the air with calls and shaping the islandâs ecology.
Then came the rats. Introduced centuries ago by ships, brown rats (Rattus norvegicus) found an island paradise with no natural predators. 
They multiplied rapidly, feeding on seabird eggs, chicks and even adults in some cases. Over time, many birds stopped returning to nest, or raised far fewer young.
By 2000, the situation was dire. Puffin surveys counted only 13 individuals, a fraction of historical levels. Other seabirds had also declined sharply, and the islandâs reputation as a seabird stronghold was at risk.
The decision to eradicate rats
Conservationists realised that without addressing the rat problem, seabird recovery on Lundy was unlikely. In 2002, the Lundy Field Society, The Landmark Trust (which manages the island) and partner organisations launched a rat-eradication project. The goal was clear: remove every rat from the island and keep it rat-free, allowing seabirds to nest without constant predation.
The operation was complex and sensitive. Lundy is not only a wildlife reserve, but a place to live, visit and bring livestock. Any eradication method had to be effective against rats, but also reduce risks to non-target species, people and pets. After careful planning, teams used a combination of baiting strategies, monitoring and strict biosecurity measures to target the rat population across the entire island.
Life after rats
Once rat numbers dropped and the island was declared rat-free, the ecological response began almost immediately. Seabirds that had avoided Lundy for years started to return. Burrows that had sat empty for decades were reoccupied. Chick survival rates improved dramatically, as eggs and nestlings were no longer being eaten overnight.
Puffins, once reduced to just 13 individuals, showed one of the most dramatic recoveries. Recent surveys count around 1,335 puffins on Lundy, a more than 100-fold increase from the low point in 2000. These birds now dig burrows in the islandâs soil, raise chicks and return year after year, forming one of the healthiest puffin colonies in the region.
A seabird powerhouse again
The recovery extends far beyond puffins. Today, more than 40,000 seabirds nest on Lundy each year, representing a wide range of species. These include: guillemots and razorbills crowd the cliff ledges, laying their eggs on narrow rock shelves; manx shearwaters return at night to their burrows, filling the darkness with eerie calls; storm petrels, one of Europeâs smallest seabirds, breed in hidden crevices and burrows; and kittiwakes, fulmars and other species add to the noise and activity during the breeding season.
For researchers and visitors, the island once again feels like a living seabird city, with constant movement between sea and shore.
Keeping Lundy rat-free
Eradicating rats was only the first step; keeping them off the island is an ongoing challenge. Rats can arrive on visiting boats, in cargo or on drifting debris. Lundy has tough biosecurity protocols to guard against reinvasion:
All incoming vessels and supplies are checked for rodents.
We also placed traps and monitoring stations around the island to catch any new rat activity early on.
Residents, staff and visitors are trained to report signs of rats immediately.
This vigilance is essential. A single breeding pair of rats could, within a few years, rebuild a population large enough to threaten seabirds again. The decades of work since 2002 depend on continued care and attention.
Why Lundy matters for conservation
Lundyâs story has become a reference point for island conservation around the world. Thousands of islands face similar problems: invasive rats, cats, mice and other predators driving declines in native birds, reptiles and invertebrates. Lundy shows that: Large-scale rat eradication is feasible on inhabited islands with careful planning and community support; seabird populations can rebound quickly once predation pressure is removed; and long-term biosecurity is as important as the initial eradication effort.
The project has inspired similar work on other UK islands and beyond, where conservationists are using Lundyâs experience to design their own eradications and restorations.
A living laboratory for researchers
For scientists, Lundy is now a living laboratory. Researchers study how seabird colonies recover over time and what factors influence their growth; hw the removal of rats affects other parts of the ecosystem, from insects to vegetation; and how best to monitor and maintain rat-free status on inhabited islands.
The islandâs long-term data setsâspanning decades before and after rat eradicationâare invaluable for understanding ecological change and refining conservation methods.
For visitors: Front row seat to recovery
Lundy offers visitors a rare chance to see success in conservation in the making. During the breeding season, birds crowd the cliffs and slopes:
From the designated paths you can see puffins diving for fish and feeding their chicks.
The ledges are crowded with guillemots and razorbills, their black and white bodies contrasting with the rock.
At night, the air fills with the calls of shearwaters and petrels returning from the sea.
Interpretive signs and guided walks help visitors understand the islandâs history, the impact of rats and the ongoing work to protect seabirds.
A second chance for an island ecosystem
In 2000, Lundyâs seabird colonies were on the brink. Puffins numbered just 13, and the islandâs reputation as a seabird haven was fading. Two decades after the rat-eradication project began, the picture is transformed: 1,335 puffins and more than 40,000 nesting seabirds have turned Lundy back into one of the UKâs most important seabird islands.
The story is a reminder that some of the most powerful conservation actions are also the simplest in concept: remove the key threat, protect the gains and let nature recover. On Lundy, that approach has given an entire island ecosystem a second chanceâone that continues to unfold with every returning seabird.
summary: Following the launch of an ambitious rat-eradication project on the island of Lundy in 2002, local seabird populations have experienced a remarkable recovery. Invasive brown rats, which were introduced centuries ago, had decimated the island's wildlife by preying on eggs, chicks, and adults. Over two decades later, strict biosecurity and the removal of predators have allowed puffins to surge from just 13 individuals in 2000 to 1,335, with over 40,000 seabirds now nesting on the island annually.
key_points: Invasive brown rats devastated Lundy's seabirds, reducing puffin numbers to a mere 13 individuals by the year 2000.
A comprehensive rat-eradication project was initiated in 2002 by conservation organizations and island management.
Puffin numbers rebounded to 1,335 individuals, and over 40,000 seabirds now nest on the island each year.
Strict ongoing biosecurity protocols, cargo checks, and traps are utilized to prevent the reinvasion of rats.
Lundy serves as a global reference point and living laboratory demonstrating the success of island conservation and ecosystem restoration.

title: Small asteroid impact today over the ocean near Australia
author: Kelly Kizer Whitt
content:
Small asteroid impact today over the ocean near Australia
![Earth as seen from space on the right with a small rocky body on the left.](https://earthsky.org/upl/2026/06/batman111-asteroid-Pixabay-e1782220671167.jpg)
Small asteroid impact today near Australia
The Mount Lemmon Observatory, as part of the Catalina Sky Survey, has spotted a new asteroid – approximately 1 meter across (around 3 feet across) – that’s headed for Earth. The impact should happen in Earth’s atmosphere near northwest Australia at 16:07 UTC (11:07 a.m. CDT). At that time near Australia the skies should be dark, so people in the area could see a bright flash of the incoming meteor.
At the moment, the asteroid has the name CERNQ52.
This is the 13th time we’ve discovered an asteroid before impact.
Richard Moissl, the Head of Planetary Defense for ESA, wrote on social media:
INCOMING! Our systems have calculated an atmospheric entry in the timeframe between 16:00-16:30 UTC of a harmless object discovered by Mt Lemmon survey with a diameter of ~0.8 m northwest of Australia over the ocean. The impact will likely cause a bright meteor.
Adrien Coffinet, a member of the Minor Planet Mailing List, wrote:
If I’m not wrong, this will be the first Aten asteroid (a < 1 AU) detected in space before impact. All the previous impactors detected in space before impact were Apollo asteroids (a > 1 AU).
Aten asteroids are those that have an orbit inside Earth’s, so under 1 astronomical unit (AU). Apollo asteroids are those that are farther from the sun than Earth on average.
![Map of world with red triangle where it was discovered and blue streak near Australia for impact.](https://earthsky.org/upl/2026/09/CERNQ52-impactor-Sep-6-2025-Richard-Moissl-e1788696334545.jpeg)
Report the meteor if you see it
If you live in the area and see the bright flash of the meteor from the asteroid impact, you can report it with the International Meteor Organization. And if you capture an image of it, share it with us at EarthSky Community Photos!
? ASTEROID ATMOSPHERIC ENTRY ALERT ?A freshly discovered (08h45min UT, Sept. 6) small (~0,8 m diameter) asteroid (CERNQ52) is in a trajectory that will direct it into the Earth atmosphere, over Indian ocean today (Sept. 6) around 16h 35min UT. Stay tuned for more updates!
— International Meteor Organization (@imometeors.bsky.social) 2026-09-06T10:45:09.571Z
Bottom line: A small asteroid impact will occur in the next few hours near northwest Australia. The meteor should harmlessly burn up in Earth’s atmosphere and poses no danger.
summary: A small asteroid named CERNQ52, measuring approximately 0.8 to 1 meter across, is on a trajectory to enter Earth's atmosphere over the ocean northwest of Australia. Discovered by the Mount Lemmon Observatory, the harmless object is expected to produce a bright meteor flash visible in the dark skies of the impact region. This marks the 13th time an asteroid has been detected in space prior to hitting Earth.
key_points: A small asteroid designated CERNQ52 is entering Earth's atmosphere near northwest Australia.
The harmless object measures roughly 0.8 to 1 meter in diameter and is expected to create a bright meteor flash.
This is the 13th time an asteroid has been successfully discovered prior to impact.
Observers in the region can report sightings to the International Meteor Organization.

title: Astronomers spot small asteroid on course to enter earth’s atmosphere
author: Gulftoday
content:
Astronomers spot small asteroid on course to enter earth’s atmosphere
Last updated: September 6, 2026 | 21:28
The photo has been used for illustrative purposes.
Maitha Al Mareekhi, Staff Reporter
Engineer Mohammed Shawkat Odeh, Director of the International Astronomical Centre (IAC), said that astronomers detected a small object, temporarily named CERNQ52, on September 6, 2026. Subsequent trajectory analyses reveal that this object is on a course towards Earth's atmosphere, anticipated to enter within hours of being spotted.
He noted that the discovery was made by the Mount Lemmon Survey in Arizona. Information released by the European Space Agency's Near-Earth Object Coordination Centre estimates the object's diameter to be between 0.6 and 1.2 meters. As per one of the most recent calculations, its entry into the atmosphere is expected between 16:07 and 16:12 GMT. However, these predictions may change with the addition of new observations.
He mentioned that some estimates suggested the entry would occur between 16:00 and 16:35 GMT, over the Indian Ocean, near northwestern Australia. This was expected to create a meteor or a very bright fireball, especially since the area would be in darkness at that time.
There is no need for concern due to the asteroid's small size; it does not pose a threat to the population. Most of it is expected to disintegrate as it enters the atmosphere, though there is a chance that small fragments might survive as meteorite debris.
He further noted that the scientific significance lies in astronomers' ability to detect this object just hours before its entry into the atmosphere and continue updating its trajectory with new observations. Initial reports suggest it could be the first known Aten class object detected in space before hitting Earth, although final orbital classification is still pending.
summary: Astronomers detected a small asteroid, temporarily named CERNQ52, on a trajectory to enter Earth's atmosphere just hours after its discovery. Measuring between 0.6 and 1.2 meters in diameter, the object does not pose a threat to the population and is expected to mostly disintegrate upon entry. The event highlights the scientific capability to detect such objects shortly before impact and refine their trajectories.
key_points: The small asteroid CERNQ52 was discovered by the Mount Lemmon Survey in Arizona on September 6, 2026.
The European Space Agency estimated the object's diameter to be between 0.6 and 1.2 meters.
Due to its small size, the asteroid does not pose a threat and is expected to mostly burn up in the atmosphere.
Initial reports suggest CERNQ52 could be the first known Aten class object detected in space before hitting Earth.
